books.description: John Donne (1572-1631) was an English poet, scholar, soldier and secretary. He is considered the pre-eminent representative of the metaphysical poets.

books.authorProfile: John Donne (1572–1631), an English poet and the pre-eminent representative of the metaphysical poets. His writing is known for intellectual argument, dramatic voice, wit, paradox, and extended metaphysical conceits.

books.readingNotes: Measured and contemplative, but never flat. Use intelligent rhetorical emphasis, subtle emotional warmth, natural breath at line endings, and slightly longer pauses between stanzas. Preserve Donne's wit, argument, tension, and sensual or devotional energy as the text requires. Use clear modern English pronunciation while respecting archaic words.
books.readingScene: A quiet wood-paneled reading room with close, warm acoustics.
books.readerProfile: A seasoned reader of English metaphysical poetry performing John Donne for an attentive, intimate audience.

books.name: Walt Whitman
books.title: Leaves of Grass
books.subtitle: A Collection from Project Gutenberg
books.description: Walt Whitman (1819-1892) was an American poet, essayist and journalist. Leaves of Grass grew across nine editions from 1855 until his death, and its long unrhymed line reshaped American poetry.
books.chatContext: Walt Whitman · Leaves of Grass · Project Gutenberg
books.sourceNote: Leaves of Grass, by Walt Whitman (1855-1892), Project Gutenberg ebook 1322
books.authorProfile: Walt Whitman (1819–1892), an American poet, essayist, and journalist, and the central figure of nineteenth-century American verse. His writing is known for the long unrhymed line, expansive catalogues, democratic and bodily celebration, direct address to the reader, and a prophetic, oratorical voice.
books.sourceProfile: Leaves of Grass, the complete 1891-92 arrangement, made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1322.
books.readingNotes: Expansive and unhurried, with the momentum of spoken oratory. Let the long lines run without chopping them, breathe at the commas of a catalogue, and build gradually through an accumulating list. Preserve Whitman's exuberance, tenderness, and direct address to the listener. Use clear modern American pronunciation.
books.readingScene: An open room with air and space around the voice, as if addressing a gathered crowd.
books.readerProfile: A seasoned reader of nineteenth-century American poetry performing Walt Whitman for an attentive audience.

books.name: Baudelaire · Huneker
books.title: The Poems and Prose Poems of Charles Baudelaire
books.subtitle: English translations, edited by James Huneker (1919)
books.description: Charles Baudelaire (1821-1867) was a French poet whose Les Fleurs du Mal found beauty in the modern city, in boredom, decay and desire, and set the course of European modernism. This edition gathers verse translations by several hands alongside the prose poems.
books.chatContext: Charles Baudelaire · Huneker edition · Project Gutenberg
books.sourceNote: The Poems and Prose Poems of Charles Baudelaire, edited by James Huneker (1919), Project Gutenberg ebook 36287
books.authorProfile: Charles Baudelaire (1821–1867), a French poet, critic, and translator, and the pivotal figure between Romanticism and modernism. His writing is known for the imagery of the modern city, the pairing of beauty with decay, spleen and ennui, synaesthesia and correspondence, and an unflinching treatment of desire and mortality. IMPORTANT: the reader sees an English translation, not Baudelaire's French. Discuss the translated text in front of you, and when the wording matters say plainly that it is a translator's choice rather than Baudelaire's own word.
books.sourceProfile: The Poems and Prose Poems of Charles Baudelaire, with an introductory preface by James Huneker (New York: Brentano's, 1919), made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/36287. The verse is rendered by several translators; the volume also contains the prose poems of Petits Poèmes en Prose.
books.readingNotes: Sensuous and controlled, with a dark elegance. Hold the long sentences together, let the imagery land without hurrying past it, and keep irony dry rather than theatrical. Preserve the tension between beauty and disgust that the poems live on. Pronounce French names and titles correctly.
books.readingScene: A shuttered nineteenth-century room, close and slightly airless, with warm dampened acoustics.
books.readerProfile: A seasoned reader of French poetry in English translation performing Baudelaire for an attentive, intimate audience.

books.name: Shakespeare
books.title: Shakespeare's Soliloquies
books.subtitle: Forty-one speeches from eight plays
books.description: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) wrote his greatest introspection not as lyric but as speech: a character alone on stage, thinking aloud. These are the best-known soliloquies from eight plays, taken from the Complete Works.
books.chatContext: William Shakespeare · Complete Works · Project Gutenberg
books.sourceNote: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, Project Gutenberg ebook 100
books.authorProfile: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), English playwright and poet. IMPORTANT: each text here is a soliloquy, a speech delivered by a character alone on stage within a play, not a lyric poem in the poet's own voice. Read it as that character speaking at that moment: attend to who is listening, what has just happened, what the speaker wants, and where they are deceiving themselves or the audience. Never treat the speaker's opinions as Shakespeare's own. The play, speaker, act, and scene are given with each speech; use them.
books.sourceProfile: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, made available by Project Gutenberg at https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/100. Each speech is taken from that text exactly as printed, including its archaic spellings and elisions. Line numbering and act or scene divisions follow that edition and may differ from others.
books.readingNotes: Perform it as a character thinking aloud, not as a recitation. Let the argument turn and change direction as it does on the page, sustain the verse line without singsong, and let pauses fall where the thought breaks rather than at every line ending. Keep the archaic elisions as written.
books.readingScene: A bare stage with a live room around the voice, an audience present but unaddressed.
books.readerProfile: A classically trained actor performing a soliloquy, intimate and unforced, thinking the words rather than declaiming them.
